# Reading the "My module this week" page: a guide for lecturers

Personal portfolio project on public UK distance-learning data; not affiliated with or endorsed by ITE or the Open
University. This is a sample of the training material that would go with such a page. The report has not been
rendered in Power BI; the static preview in `dashboard/preview.html` shows the same figures.

<!-- Generated by scripts/build_docs.py from results/*.json. Edit docs/templates/lecturer_guide.md instead. -->

## What the page is for

One job: helping you decide which students to get in touch with this week. It does not grade students and it does
not predict anyone's future.

Pick your module and a cut-off day at the top. Everything on the page then shows what was known at the end of the
day before the cut-off. Students who had already withdrawn by then, or had not yet registered, are not listed.

## The five numbers at the top

| Number | What it counts | How to read it |
|---|---|---|
| Students | Students registered at the cut-off | Your class size for this view |
| Flagged Students | The fifth of the class with the highest risk scores | A shortlist sized to what one person can follow up; the size is fixed, so it says nothing about whether the class is doing well |
| Inactive Students | No clicks at all in the last two weeks | The plainest warning sign there is. Across the data, students with no clicks in the two weeks before day 28 were at risk {{descriptive.json:associations_day_28.0.risk_ratio|.1f}} times as often as the rest |
| Students Missing an Assessment | At least one assessment was due and was not handed in | Results carried over from an earlier attempt count as handed in |
| Average Score | Mean of students' average scores so far | Blank early in term, before anything has been marked |

## The two charts

- **Share of enrolled students active online, by week.** Of the students registered at the start of each week, the
  share who clicked at least once. A falling line is normal after the first weeks; a sudden drop in one week is
  worth a look (a holiday, an outage, a deadline elsewhere). This chart shows the whole term and does not change
  with the cut-off.
- **Where the clicks went.** The split between course content, forums, quizzes and the module homepage. It shows
  what the class uses, not how well anyone is learning.

## The student table

One row per student, highest risk score first. Students are shown by a code, not a name.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Risk score | A number between 0 and 1 from a model trained on the previous year's classes. Use it to order the list. Do not quote it to a student and do not read 0.7 as "70% likely to fail" |
| Flagged | 1 for the top fifth of your class |
| Days since last active | Days since the student was last seen online |
| Clicks last 2 weeks, Assessments missed, Average score | The facts behind the score |
| Reasons | Up to three plain statements of what pushed this student's score up, for flagged students only |

## What a flag means, and what it does not

A flag means: **among your students, this one's recent activity and assessment record look most like those of
earlier students who went on to withdraw or fail.**

How often is it right? On the 2014 classes in this data, at day 28:

- of the students flagged when one in five is flagged,
  {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.logistic_regression.top20.precision|pct0}} did go on to withdraw or fail. So roughly
  one flagged student in four was fine;
- the flagged group contained {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.logistic_regression.top20.recall|pct0}} of all the
  students who went on to withdraw or fail. So most students who struggled were **not** on the list.

A flag does not mean:

- that the student will fail. Many flagged students pass;
- that an unflagged student is safe. The list is short by design;
- that the reasons shown are causes. "Few clicks" describes what the model saw; it does not say why;
- anything about ability, motivation or character.

The model was not given gender, age, disability, home region or deprivation band. It can still treat groups
differently through the behaviour it does see; the README reports those gaps.

## What to do next

1. Start with flagged students who are also inactive or have missed an assessment: two independent signs.
2. Use what you know that the data does not: a student who told you about a hospital stay does not need a warning.
3. Make contact as an offer of help, not as a notice. Do not mention a score or a flag.
4. Note what you did and what you learned, wherever your college records such contact. Without that, nobody can
   find out whether the list helps.
5. Tell the data team when the list is wrong in the same way twice. That is how it improves.

## Limits you should know about

- The page is built on clicks and submitted work. It sees nothing of attendance, practical work, conversations or
  life outside the course.
- The model was trained on a UK distance-learning university in 2013. It has not been checked on any other
  institution and should not be assumed to hold elsewhere.
- Scores are treated as known on the day work is handed in. In practice marking takes time.
- Early in term there is little to go on: at day 14 the list is right less often than at day 28
  ({{model.json:cutoffs.14.models.logistic_regression.top20.precision|pct0}} of flagged students at risk, against
  {{model.json:cutoffs.28.models.logistic_regression.top20.precision|pct0}}).
